newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bourse drifts with U.S. and UK markets.
newsitem.headline: Irish bourse drifts with U.S. and UK markets.

text.p: The Irish bourse ended marginally down in thin trading on Thursday in sympathy with unsettled UK and U.S. markets, dealers said.

"The market was weaker in the leaders today, with the banks and CRH selling off, mainly due to weaker results from the UK and the U.S. coming through this afternoon," a dealer said. "We saw some two-way trade but volume wasn't impressive."
Markets on both sides of the Atlantic were unsettled by worries about a possible near-term U.S. interest rate hike. Weaker bond markets also weighed on share prices.
Dealers said Smurfit remained the best bid of the larger stocks, but second-line industrials were also still attracting strong bids.
"There are sellers around in some of the food stocks but generally people are trying to get money into the smaller names," a dealer said.

Irish financial services group Woodchester Investments Plc, which added 15 pence to its share price after news this morning that the group may become a takeover target, fell back five pence to 285 amid restrained trade in the afternoon, dealers said.

Woodchester earlier announced that Credit Lyonnais will sell its 54 percent shareholding in the group once it receives a price which reflects the full value of its interest. The move is expected to lead to a full bid for Woodchester.
Woodchester also reported a 22 percent rise in 1996 pre-tax profits to 44 million Irish pounds earlier.
Among leading financials AIB fell four pence to 449, Bank of Ireland dropped four pence to 648, while Irish Life was off one pence at 330, and Irish Permanent was down two pence at 623.
Among leading industrials, food stock Avonmore remained unchanged at 235 while CRH fell five pence to 647. Kerry Group was flat at 660.
By 1710 GMT, the ISEQ index of Irish shares was down 13.38 points or 0.44 percent at 3,042.13.

Elsewhere the FTSE 100 and the Dow both followed bonds down in the wake of a stronger-than-expected U.S. retail sales report. Sales rose by 0.8 percent in February, 0.2 percent above Wall Street estimates, after a revised 1.5 percent jump in January.
The strength in U.S. sales fanned concerns that the Federal Open Market Committee, the policy-making arm of the Federal Reserve, may tighten credit at its next meeting on March 25, dealers said.
